title: Venezuela’s Acting Leader Makes Her U.N. Debut
gist: Latin America Brief: acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez addressed UNGA and met Trump while giving no election timeline, as the U.S. works with her to rebuild Venezuela's oil industry and regional leaders normalize her rule. Also: Guyana's 33.3% H1 GDP growth on Iran-war oil prices, a new $100m development bank, the UN secretary-general race, and a crypto-backed AI governance city project in Uruguay.

insights.claim: The Trump administration is working with acting President Delcy Rodríguez to rebuild Venezuela's oil industry after the U.S. military captured Maduro in January.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: U.S.-backed Venezuelan oil recovery is a supply-side factor for heavy crude markets.
insights.quote: Meanwhile, the Trump administration is working with Rodríguez on efforts to rebuild the country’s oil industry.
insights.locator: Maduro returned to New York this year

insights.claim: Despite polls showing Venezuelans overwhelmingly want free elections, neither Rodríguez nor the U.S. has given a timeline, suggesting Trump is in no rush for elections.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Implies a stable, U.S.-aligned transitional regime is the base case for oil investment, with political legitimacy risk.
insights.quote: Altogether, the events suggest that Trump is in no rush for elections in Venezuela—and that Trump-friendly presidents in the region are not pushing for democratization, either.

insights.claim: Regional leaders are normalizing Rodríguez: Paraguay's Peña visited Caracas and Chile's Kast met her, while Panama's Mulino brushed off questions about opposition leader Machado, who has been repeatedly blocked from returning.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Diplomatic normalization lowers political-risk barriers to re-engagement with Venezuela.

insights.claim: Venezuela produces an estimated 1.2 million barrels per day.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Baseline for gauging recovery of Venezuelan output.

insights.claim: Guyana reported 33.3 percent GDP growth in the first half of 2026, supercharged by high oil prices from the Iran war, and now produces about 900,000 barrels per day for roughly 1 million people.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Guyana is a major non-OPEC supply growth story and beneficiary of the war-driven price spike.
insights.quote: Last week, oil-rich Guyana announced dramatic economic growth numbers for the first half of 2026: a 33.3 percent GDP expansion.

insights.claim: Guyana is launching a development bank with $100 million in capital for small no-interest loans, adding to free tuition and one-time $500 cash transfers, amid criticism of the low government take from oil companies.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Pressure on oil revenue distribution could eventually raise fiscal-terms risk for operators.

insights.claim: Political pushback in Guyana is building: a new opposition party became second-largest in the legislature and anti-government protests followed a deadly ferry capsizing in July.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Rising political risk could lead to renegotiation pressure on oil contracts.

insights.claim: Guyana poverty estimates range from over 50 percent (IDB, 2024) to 18-20 percent (local analysts), and the government does not regularly publish poverty data.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Data gaps obscure how much oil wealth reaches citizens, a governance risk indicator.

insights.claim: Trump-friendly Latin American leaders at a 'Shield of the Americas' event agreed to explore sanctioning drug gangs and designating them as terrorists, meaning more governments could use their armies to fight crime and allow U.S. partners to join.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Militarized anti-cartel policy raises regional security operations and potential for U.S. strikes.
insights.quote: The move means that more Latin American governments could soon use their armies to fight crime—and allow U.S. partners to join.

insights.claim: Michelle Bachelet withdrew from the UN secretary-general race; the two front-runners in Security Council straw polls, Rebeca Grynspan and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, are both Latin American.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Signals direction of UN leadership, marginal for markets.

insights.claim: Crypto-funded online community Praxis says members will move to a yet-to-be-built AI-governed city in Uruguay within the +Colonia development, underscoring the Southern Cone's draw for U.S. tech utopians.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
insights.so_what: Niche signal of crypto/AI capital flowing to Southern Cone charter-city projects.
